Question: Can the existence of God be proven? If it were possible, what would be the implications and what could potentially exist beyond our universe?
Answer: If God actually behaved as portrayed in the Bible, then yes, his existence absolutely could be proven. Question: If atheism is true, why are there still monkeys? I thought monkeys evolved into humans over billions of years.
Answer: The broad pattern of evolution is diversification to take advantage of new and varied ecological niches. Just for a moment, consider birds, and how many different species of birds there are today. You probably wouldn’t ask why other birds are still around if golden eagles evolved from birds. It hopefully seems obvious that golden eagles aren’t the only successful lifestyle for birds, and that there are lots of other ways for other bird species to survive without becoming more like golden eagles. In fact, it’s downright advantageous. There are only so many resources to go around in the golden eagle niche, so it’s better for other bird species to find other ways to make a living to have access to different resources. A hummingbird doesn’t have to compete with a golden eagle for food, while penguins can survive in environments that would kill eagles. It’s the same way with so many other branches of life, from beetles to ants to rodents to us monkeys. Successful lineages branch out and become more diverse, as they split up into more and more species to take advantage of more opportunities. Here’s a high level family tree of primates: ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982212008068 Now sure, you can play semantic games over whether those ‘Early simians’ should be called monkeys or not, but I think if we had a time machine and could bring one to the present, most people would think of it as a monkey. And monkeys have been a successful enough lineage that modern day monkeys have diversified into hundreds of species, from New World monkeys to Old World monkeys to apes, and yes, that includes us humans, as well. In other words, there are still other monkeys besides people because monkeys are a successful lineage, and there are lots of niches that they’ve evolved to take advantage of. Just to clarify, from those earliest monkeys to us humans has only taken tens of millions of years, not billions. And I know there are also more semantics around whether apes are monkeys or not, but I’ve come around to the idea that ‘monkey’ should be a monophyletic group, and that us apes should just be considered as a branch of monkeys.

Question: Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible?
Answer: It really does come from the Bible, if a bit indirectly. There are several passages in the Bible that give information on such things as how old people were when they had children or how long certain periods lasted, that if accepted at face value, can give a very close approximation of when Adam and Eve were created (according to the stories, at least). There are a few places where things get somewhat murky, but not enough to change things by more than a few decades* – nothing on the order of millions or billions of years. This was a fairly well accepted interpretation for generations, and many scholars made their own estimates of when creation would have taken place, including Johannes Kepler. Arguably the most respected of these was the estimate done by James Ussher, who put much effort into sorting out the murky periods. It's because Ussher's chronology was so well respected that it was included in the introductory material to several printed Bibles, including the famed Scofield Bible. Wikipedia gives a good summary of how Ussher made his estimate (Ussher chronology - Wikipedia). He broke it down into three periods: Using other sources outside the Bible, Ussher determined the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Creation to Exodus You can easily look up Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 for yourself, but to give an idea, here's the start of Genesis 5: This is the list of the descendants of Adam. When God created humans,[a] he made them[b] in the likeness of God. 2 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called them humans[c] when they were created. 3 When Adam had lived one hundred thirty years, he became the father of a son in his likeness, according to his image, and named him Seth. 4 The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters. 5 Thus all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, and he died. 6 When Seth had lived one hundred five years, he became the father of Enosh. 7 Seth lived after the birth of Enosh eight hundred seven years and had other sons and daughters. 8 Thus all the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, and he died. It goes on and on like that. So, as long as you accept these statements as true, it's mostly a simple matter of adding up how old each man was when he begat his heir. The only real hiccups are between Noah and Shem, and between Nahor and Terah. Both of these are somewhat ambiguous. In the former, the passage states, "After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth." In the latter, the passage is, "When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran." People who care about this issue more than I do have gone into detail to try to pinpoint those ages (e.g. Contradictions: Noah’s Three Sons). You also need to know how old Abraham was when the Exodus occurred. His age at the start of all those events comes from Genesis 12:4, "So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran." I ran the math myself with a spreadsheet, and came up with 2049 years from the creation of Adam to the birth of Abraham, plus another 75 years until the Exodus, for 2124 years total (a bit different from Ussher because I didn't put in the effort to figure out the ambiguity around Noah/Shem and Nahor/Terah). I suppose there's one other hiccup, depending on which particular version of the Bible you're using. Since we don't have an 'original' version of Genesis, we have to rely on copies of that version, most notably the Masoretic text and the Septuagint (though those aren't the only two). And those copies differ on certain details, including all those ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. Exodus to Solomon's Temple Like I said, this one comes straight from a single verse, 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity This is the period where things purportedly get a bit more complicated. I haven't gone through this period in detail, yet, myself, but to give just one example, you have this verse from 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. Go through finding all those verses and work out the years, and you come up a little over 4 centuries of history. In a somewhat independent path, other books in the Bible also give more genealogies, such that you can trace each and every claimed descendant from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, there aren't ages associated with all of those genealogies, but these also give a ballpark range in the thousands of years. So, if you accept the claims of the Bible at more or less face value, and assume all those genealogies represent real people and not just imaginary people made up out of thin air, and that all the events in Egypt, Israel, and Judah all really happened, you'll end up at an estimate for the date of creation somewhere around 4000 BC. As a side note, while it seems to be somewhat fashionable to dismiss exercises like these because some parts of the Bible were ‘obviously’ meant to be taken more metaphorically or allegorically, I don’t see such figurative interpretations as obvious at all. The crux of this argument would be the genealogies in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 – after that, you’re already into Egyptian pharaohs, so nothing that’s going to be a major difference from real history (at least as far as timelines). But these genealogies aren’t fables with moral lessons or some type of simplified explanation of complex concepts for a pre-scientific society. They’re boring, dry lists of ancestry. It’s about as close to a conventional history section as you’ll find in Genesis – the part least likely to be metaphorical or allegorical (though there’s certainly a reason to ‘invent’ such lists to provide legitimacy for the rulers of Israel and Judah). *As I already touched upon, that difference of only a few decades is using a specific version of the Bible, such as the Masoretic text or the Septuagint. The differences between those different versions can add up to a couple millennia, though still not anywhere near on the magnitude of real history.

Question: If atheists begin to believe in my god, what would they lose? They will not lose anything.
Answer: Your god must be the least demanding one out there, because a lot of the gods people believe in aren’t so laid back. For many Christians, there's the 10% tithe right off the bat. Back when I was still religious and my wife and I were looking for a church in town, one actually wanted to see our pay stubs so that they knew how much to extort from us each week. Sorry – I mean, how much we would 'donate'. Then there's the time investment. That's at least a couple hours every Sunday when I could be doing something else. Then there are lost opportunities. Muslims and Jews, for example, would deprive me of bacon cheeseburgers. Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, and Sikhism would deprive me of meat entirely. Southern Baptists would have me abstain from alcohol. Mormons would take that even further and have me abstain from even coffee and Diet Coke. Then you get into more serious issues like abortion rights for women, marriage equality and other civil rights for LGBTQ+ folks, Catholics' weird hang-ups against condoms which has exacerbated the HIV crisis in Africa, and on and on. And although I don’t want to discuss supernatural aspects too much since I don’t believe in any of them, what if you’ve picked the wrong god to believe in? If you want me to be a Christian but the ancient Egyptians were right, then I won’t know any of the spells to guide me to Field of Reeds. If the ancient Greeks were right, where would I get my coins to cross the River Styx? If Hindus are right, then following some of the more hateful forms of Christianity might screw up my karma and yield me a pretty bad life in my next reincarnation. I know, not every religion has every one of these issues. But there are plenty of costs and negative impacts that can come from certain specific religions. And when you look at that in comparison to the likelihood of Bronze Age to Iron Age mythology actually being true, well, I'm not going to lose any sleep over ordering a bacon cheeseburger and a pint at a bar in the middle of a pride rally.

Question: Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why?
Answer: I'm going to focus on this part of your question: As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. No, you don't. I studied Spanish pretty extensively in high school and college, to the point of being only 2 classes away from a Spanish minor*. I could speak fairly fluently. Then, after I graduated, I met the woman who was to become my wife, who happens to be Mexican with a large Mexican family (all living in the U.S.). I could catch them making grammatical 'errors' that weren't 'proper' Spanish**, and I could definitely spell Spanish words better than them (they mostly grew up in the U.S., so didn't have much formal education in Spanish). But my way of speaking Spanish was much more academic and stuffy, and just didn't flow the same way. Nobody would have confused me as speaking better Spanish than native speakers who had been speaking it their entire lives. Going the other way, I once made a business trip to China, and during the one day we set aside for sight seeing, I was approached by an old Chinese guy who wanted to speak to me in English, who turned out to be a retired English teacher. In other words, he was such an expert in the English language among the Chinese that he was teaching others how to speak English. But his English wasn't exactly the best. Don't get me wrong, his English was far better than my non-existent skills in Chinese, but it seemed obvious that he'd probably never been outside China and gotten to practice with actual native speakers. Even a lifetime of academic study isn't enough to make someone speak as well as a native speaker. Now, I really suspect you're a troll and not somebody who just began studying English 3 months ago. But people who aren't native speakers have to study a long, long, long time to become as proficient at the language as native speakers. And it really requires immersion in the culture, hearing the language day in and day out to pick up all the nuances and informalities that you simply can't completely learn any other way. On the off chance that you really are new to studying English, learn a bit of humility like I did when I met my wife’s family. Academic English is not the way real people speak, and it’s going to take a lot more than three months of studying in a school environment before you sound natural. *The reason I didn't just tack on two more classes was because I was already taking one Spanish class my final semester, and another two would have given me a very full load. So, instead, I tacked on a semester of Italian to learn a bit more of a different language. I figured the actual skill would serve me better than an additional piece of paper. **I put grammatical 'errors' in scare quotes, because I've come around to the idea of grammar being descriptive, not prescriptive. Who gets to decide what's proper and what's not. Where do they get off thinking they have that authority? Language has been around for far longer than scholars to study it, and people did just fine.

Question: Is the Fahrenheit temperature scale calibrated so that 0 or 100 are meaningful (to something other than water)?
Answer: In a paper that Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit submitted to the Royal Society, he explained for himself the three points originally used to calibrate his thermometers (though in principle, only two points should have been required). If you can read Latin, the full paper is available here: Otherwise, you can find an English translation of a relevant portion here: Here is how he defined each point: The first is found in the uncalibrated part or the beginning of the scale, and is determined by a mixture of ice, water and ammonium chloride or even sea salt. If the thermometer is placed in this mixture, its liquid descends as far as the degree that is marked with a zero. The second point is obtained if water and ice are mixed without the aforementioned salts. When the thermometer is placed in this mixture, its liquid reaches the 32nd degree. I call this ‘freezing point’. The third point is situated at the 96th degree. Alcohol expands up to this point when it is held in the mouth or under the armpit of a living man in good health until it has completely acquired his body heat. So, zero was the lowest temperature easily achievable in a lab, with just water, ice, and salt. The upper point of human body temperature was set at 96°, which for people already used to traditional measurements is a nice, even eight dozen. From there, it seems that Anders Celsius's work had a major influence to use the freezing and boiling points of water (at standard pressure) as the main calibration points. So using the already defined 32° for the freezing point of pure water, Fahrenheit's scale was tweaked just a bit to make the boiling point 212°, which meant a nice round 180° between them (or a half circle's worth of degrees). By the way, that tweak undid his 0° calibration point. In the modern day Fahrenheit scale, that brine solution sits at 4°F. So, it was a bit of a meandering development, but there was some rationale for the original calibration points. At least Fahrenheit set cold temperatures as the lower values, unlike Mr. Celsius who originally set his scale with boiling at 0° and freezing at 100°.

Question: Is music at best better than food?
Answer: It's obviously going to depend on the individual. But for me, if you gave me a choice between a flavorless nutrition pill for the rest of my life while being able to listen to any music I wanted to, vs. being able to eat whatever foods I wanted but no longer allowed to listen to music, I'd pick the food in a heartbeat. You've probably heard the expression that some people eat to live, while others live to eat. I'm firmly in the latter category. Food is just so damn good and brings so much enjoyment. Oh sure, I like music well enough. The first time I heard Sonic Youth was a revelation. But even the music I like the most doesn't bring me as much joy as good food. I mean, for one, you've got potatoes. I've written about potatoes before, so I won't dwell on it (Jeff Lewis's answer to If you had to survive on only one food, which food would it be?). But potatoes alone are enough reason to choose food over music. Then you've got things like hoagies, Reuben sandwiches, Buffalo wings, chiles rellenos, fried chicked, medium rare ribeye, stinky tofu, Peking duck with that delicious crispy skin, the simple joy of a good croissant with coffee... ABOVE SOURCE: BarnWorksDesigns.com Music is nice and all. And there are some bands that I like a lot. But I never spend any part of my day planning ahead to what music I might want to listen to later, or getting particularly excited about the prospect of hearing a particular song. But food, on the other hand... From breakfast, I'm already looking forward to lunch. From lunch, I'm already looking forward to supper. And from supper, I'm already looking forward to starting over the cycle the next day. And if it's any type of special occasion, like a party or going out to dinner, I might start getting excited about the food days in advance. Good food is one of the greatest joys in life.

Question: Is it true that the shooter at Trump's rally was a registered Republican with conservative beliefs and a gun enthusiast? Why are conservatives blaming the left for this incident?
Answer: There's simply not much to go on to identify his political leanings at this point. Back in 2021, when he was 17, he made a $15 donation to a progressive organization, ActBlue. And yes, despite online rumors, it most likely really was him. When he was old enough to vote, he registered as a Republican. This could mean he legitimately was a Republican. But given that Pennsylvania has a closed primary, this could also mean he wanted to participate in the Republican primary rather than the Democratic primary. As a liberal living in Texas with an open primary, I've voted in the Republican primary before, since I figured it was my only realistic option of trying to influence the governor's race (the Republican I preferred still lost). He seemed to like guns, trying out for his school's shooting team and being a member of a local gun range. At the time of the shooting, he was wearing a t-shirt for a gun enthusiast YouTube channel. But while enthusiasm for guns does skew a bit towards conservative political leanings, it's not at all a sure thing. I like taking my own pistol to the range, for example, and I know plenty of other liberals and Democrats who own and shoot guns. (I'll add that I've seen a few gun enthusiasts trying to use a No True Scotsman argument, claiming that a true gun enthusiast wouldn't have missed this shot, would have used a different rifle, etc. But you don't have to be an expert marksman to merely like guns and like going shooting.) In interviews with former classmates, one student who took an American history course with him stated that he "definitely was conservative", and went on to add about a mock debate that, "The majority of the class were on the liberal side, but Tom, no matter what, always stood his ground on the conservative side." But there's any number of reasons to take this hearsay with a grain of salt (the classmate could have been talking big just to get attention; he might not have known the shooter as well as he claimed, the shooter might have just enjoyed arguing, etc.) I'd also point out that people's political motivations can be quite fluid around that age. Whatever he believed at 17 might not be the same as at 18 or 20. And finally, as I've seen many others point out, we don't even know if his motivation was political. The guy who tried to assassinate Reagan did it to try to get the attention of a movie star. At this point, anybody claiming to know definitively one way or the other which way the shooter leaned politically is not looking at the evidence objectively. And it's an even bigger stretch to try to definitively claim that politics were his main motivation. Investigators are doing their best to figure out his motives. So until then, or until more public evidence comes to light, let's try to keep our speculations grounded in what's actually known. Update 2024–07–22: While it’s still a bit early to say anything definitive about the shooter, the emerging picture seems to be that he was looking for notoriety by shooting somebody famous, not any particular political leanings. In addition to Trump, he’d been searching online for Biden and other prominent political figures. The proximity of the Trump rally to his hometown seems like it might have been the biggest motivator in him choosing Trump over any of the other people he’d been considering.

Question: Is it ok for atheists to use phrases like "oh my god!", "Jesus Christ!", "what the hell?" , etc in a sentence when talking to someone?
Answer: If anything, it's less of an issue for us atheists. Christians have that whole commandment about not taking the Lord's name in vain. Back when I was still a Christian, I took that very seriously, and never would have dreamt of saying 'Oh my God' or 'Jesus Christ' as mere explitives. I mean, I knew there were much more serious issues that that commandment was referring to (What Does It Really Mean to Take the Lord’s Name in Vain?), but invoking the name of God just for emphasis on worldly concerns still fell under the rules. It's only now that I'm an atheist that I can say those expressions without fear of eternal damnation. So I sometimes do. Not because there's any mystical power about those terms in particular, but because taboo phrases carry more emotional impact than non-taboo phrases. Likewise, if I exclaim 'holy sh*t' or 'what the f*ck', I'm not literally referring to excrement or sexual intercourse. It's that those phrases carry so much emotional weight. Question: For those of you over 40, what is it that confuses you the most about young people?
Answer: Ouch. I guess you never really think of yourself as old until someone else implies it. Compared to all the greybeards in engineering, I still thought of myself as 'young'. But for the most part, I'm not really confused by all that much about younger folks. A whole lot of complaining about Millennials and Gen Z is the same old complaining the older generations have always done. I remember my grandparents complaining about my own generation. I'm sure their grandparents did the same thing. You can find this type of complaining about 'kids these days' going back thousands of years: Of course, times do change, from technologies to cultural norms to economic realities, so Millennials do things a bit differently than my generation, and Gen Z will do things a bit differently from them. But, so far at least, none of it really confuses me. It kind of reminds me of Douglas Adams quote: 1. Anything invented after you’re thirty-five is against the natural order of things. Thankfully, even though I have crossed over Adams’ 35 year mark a while back, I'm still not quite in the grumpy old man stage. But give me time.

Question: What is a creature that was believed to be alive during the dinosaur era, but we have never found it?
Answer: The one I'm most curious about is early pterosaurs. The picture we have right now from currently known fossils is something like this: ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982221009155 That’s a big jump from Lagerpetids to Preondactylus. Lagerpetids show no particular adaptations to gliding or flying, while Preondactylus was already a competent flyer. And even using Lagerpetids in that diagram is questionable – the exact group that's closest to pterosaurs is still debatable. For example, here are a few proposed relationships: ABOVE SOURCE: Pterosauromorpha - Wikipedia The first problem is that fossils are simply rare to begin with. I saw one estimate that less than 0.1% of animal species have become fossils (How can I become a fossil? ). This rarity is compounded by habitats, where in environments like forests, scavengers and decomposers consume every last bit of a dead animal and leave no trace. It’s even further compounded by the size of the animal – smaller animals have more fragile skeletons even less likely to last long enough to become fossils. So if pterosaurs first evolved in forests as small animals gliding amongst the trees, our chances of finding early pterosaurs along that transition are pretty slim. In my own lifetime, we’ve been extremely lucky to find these sorts of transitional fossils for early birds, to the point where it’s debatable about which animals could actually fly or not. But sadly, the early evolution of pterosaurs remains a mystery.

Question: ‘After-birth abortion’: Are they serious?
Answer: Well, if you look at the actual situations where this is being discussed rather than just fear mongering about imaginary situations, then yes. Nobody wants to kill a healthy late term fetus or newborn. No woman goes through 9 months of pregnancy just to decide at the last minute that she's changed her mind. And certainly no doctor would kill a healthy newborn baby after the entire process of labor or a Caesarean delivery. But not all fetuses and newborns are healthy. Hopefully, with good pre-natal care, any major complications will be detected early. But not everybody has access to the best pre-natal care, and even then, some complications simply don't get detected until late into the pregnancy. And some of these complications are euphemistically referred to as "incompatible with life". In other words, they're complications so severe that the baby won't survive even with the best medical treatment available. Trying to treat these conditions will only delay the inevitable and prolong the suffering. So, the question becomes, what truly is the most humane and merciful course of action in these cases? Prolonging suffering, or doing what you can to ease the pain and try to end the suffering as soon as possible? In another recent answer, Jeff Lewis's answer to Democrats support post-birth abortion, but isn’t abortion after birth just murder?, I discussed a study that polled "physicians and paramedical professionals involved in late TOP [termination of pregnancy] decision‐making in all eight centers with a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit in Flanders, Belgium (N = 117)". As I pointed out in that answer, "These aren't folks for whom this question is a mere hypothetical. They have to see the consequences and suffering of the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit on a daily basis." And such health care professionals were overwhelmingly in favor of "actively terminat[ing] life" for newborns with serious enough conditions. And while the support for feticide wasn't quite so overwhelming, a majority still supported feticide over palliative care in serious enough cases. So yes, sometimes the humane and merciful choice is to end a poor newborn's suffering. It's a tragedy, and would be absolutely gut wrenching to the parents (and the doctors – they're humans, too). But the alternative is just forcing the newborn to suffer longer before still eventually dying. Seriously, these are profound and extremely serious situations that some families find themselves in. Let's not take away the merciful options in an already shitty situation just so we can shout some slogans to win political points. ETA: After some feedback in the comments, I want to be very clear on this. I'm talking about newborns with severe complications and no chance of recovery. The question is what’s best for these babies, which has to be looked at on a case by case basis. Is there any quality of life at all, or just suffering? Palliative care and hospice are already available for newborns with severe complications, ranging from not attempting to treat the condition, to withholding nutrition. And quite obviously, such infants will die. But with their condition, they would have died anyway. It certainly can't be considered more humane to prolong their suffering. And that leads into the debate raised in this question, although the OP seemed disingenuous in how they framed it, of whether active feticide is an appropriate approach for these babies, or if the current standard of palliative care is sufficient (and I really, really hope you're not against palliative care – who would actually push for making babies suffer even more). As I said in my prior answer, "I understand people's hesitancy to enable doctor's to actively end the life of patients as opposed to mere palliative care, especially in the case of patients who are too young to voice their own desires." So the question comes down to balancing the best interests of babies with such severe complications vs. how comfortable we are with intentionally taking steps to end a life. Minimizing the suffering for these babies as much as possible would require active feticide. Palliative care allows people to have an easier conscience, but forces the babies to suffer a bit longer. Active attempts to treat such conditions would prolong the suffering the longest. And as I pointed out in my answer, these aren't just hypotheticals. There are real, non-thought experiment babies suffering in NICUs right now, with parents agonizing over their decisions.

Question: What are some books that every aspiring Aerospace engineer should read?
Answer: I come at this issue much more from the aero side than the space side. That said, there are a few books that I refer back to fairly often: Introduction to Flight, by John D. Anderson This is just a solid textbook on the fundamentals, with lots of interesting side notes related to aviation history. This should be the first book in your collection. You can get a good idea of the topics just from the chapter titles: 1) The First Aeronautical Engineers 2) Fundamental Thoughts 3) The Standard Atmosphere 4) Basic Aerodynamics 5) Airfoils, Wings, and Other Aerodynamics Shapes 6) Elements of Airplane Performance 7) Principles of Stability and Control 8) Space Flight (Astronautics) 9) Propulsion 10) Hypersonic Vehicles On a personal note, I'll add that Dr. Anderson is a phenomenal teacher. I had him for several of my engineering classes, as well as an honors seminar on aviation history. He gave that class a personal tour of the Air and Space Museum in D.C., which is one of the best museum visits I've ever experienced. I'll also note that my personal copy of this book is the 3rd edition, while the latest is the 9th. Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach, by Daniel P. Raymer Back when I was in my aircraft design class in college, we referred to this book as our Bible, both for its form factor and for the wealth of information it contained. There's just tons of practical information for designing aircraft. His empirical trends for aircraft weight estimates are a recognized standard. My copy of this book (3rd edition) has a ton of index cards and post it notes marking the sections that I refer back to the most often. Theory of Wing Sections, by Abbbott and Doenhoff This book is still the standard when it comes to airfoils. After that comes around 300 pages of appendices, broken down into Basic Thickness Forms, Mean Lines, Airfoil Ordinates, and finally and perhaps most usefully, Aerodynamic Characteristics, with just page after page of lift, drag, and moment curves. Question: Why do liberals claim to be Christians? They support abortion, homosexual marriage, etc. These people do not follow any of the Bible's rules, why do they still call themselves Christians? There is a word "heresy" and it applies to liberals

Or to take a far less controversial example, I didn’t expect government to outlaw consumption of meat on Fridays during Lent. That was something that I practiced, not something to be forced on others. Marriage was the same way. Jesus's Core Message At least per the Gospels, Jesus actually told his followers which commandments were the most important. I'm guessing that if you're a Christian, you already know this, but just to be thorough, here's the relevant passage from Matthew 22 (emphasis mine): When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together, and one of them, an expert in the law, asked him a question to test him. “Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?” He said to him, “ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ This is the greatest and first commandment. And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” For this answer, I want to highlight the second one, there, because that one has more implications on how people should be treating other people. In Luke 10, in a similar passage where Jesus preached the importance of loving your neighbor as yourself, he was asked a follow-up question of "And who is my neighbor?" Of course, this is where Jesus responded with the famous parable of the Good Samaritan, which culminated with this lesson: Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?” He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.” And of course, there's another famous parable from Matthew 25: Then the king will say to those at his right hand, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me.’ Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and gave you food or thirsty and gave you something to drink? And when was it that we saw you sick or in prison and visited you?’ And the king will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did it to me.’ Jesus preached caring for the hungry, the poor, the strangers in our midst, and even prisoners. SOURCE: El Paso leaders rally around migrant shelters after Attorney General Ken Paxton’s threat to shut them down I'll close this answer with a video that's a few years old, but really highlights the divide between what Jesus preached and what today's Republican Party stands for. Question: Why do so many people hate the self checkouts?
Answer: Actually, I tend to prefer it. But it really depends on the implementation, and what the store was like before they brought in the self checkouts. Let me take my local Walmart as an example. Back in the days before self checkouts, they never had enough cashiers for the number of customers. There was no such thing as a quick trip to Walmart, because you inevitably got stuck in a long line waiting to check out. Then, when they did bring in self checkouts, they brought in dozens of them. So now, there's almost always at least one self-checkout open. And even if there is a line, it's more like a bank line, where everybody waits in one line, and then just goes to the next open checkout. So it doesn't matter if there are a few folks with full carts, because they're only tying up that one particular checkout, not the entire line. Now it really is possible to be in and out of Walmart in 5 minutes if I only need one thing. I've been to other stores, though, where they've only installed a limited number of self checkouts. And the worst offenders don't even go with the bank-style lines, but have separate lines for each self checkout. Those are annoying, where you may end up waiting longer than the pre-self-checkout days. My favorite modern checkout is Sam's Club (I'd imagine the other warehouse stores have this as well, but Wichita Falls, TX doesn't give you many options). You just download an app to your phone to scan the items as you shop, swipe a button to pay with a credit card on file, and then just briefly show your phone to the receipt checker on your way out the door. It's hard to get much quicker and convenient than that. But my second favorite checkout is at a small grocery chain called United Market Street, which has a good compromise between self checkouts and old school people. They do employ plenty of real life cashiers to scan your groceries, so the lines are rarely very long. And they even still have baggers, who take your groceries out to your car for you. They also have about half a dozen self checkouts, largely to replace the express checkout. So even the express line folks don't get all that inconvenienced by somebody cheating with a cart full of 50 things. Of course, you pay for it. Their prices aren't horrible, but they're definitely higher than Walmart or Aldi. As far as a few other answers I've seen about taking away low skill jobs, meh. The recent trend of online shopping seems to have taken care of that, with employees running around to fill all those online orders. My daughter did that for a bit at the aforementioned Market Street, and I see plenty of folks with that job at my local Walmart. So, until robots take over that, those jobs offset the loss of cashiers. So as long as it's done right, and considering that stores were skimping on cashiers even before self-checkouts were a thing, I've found self-checkouts to make shopping more convenient.

Question: How can one respond to the argument that the existence of monkeys disproves the theory of evolution?
Answer: I see a lot of answers here proposing ridicule and laughter, which I think are missing a great opportunity to make somebody one of today's "lucky 10,000". ABOVE SOURCE: XKCD - Ten Thousand Anybody asking this question quite obviously didn't have the best science education growing up, so this is your chance to share the excitement of understanding a topic as enthralling as universal common descent. Anyway, as far as this particular question goes, it's been asked so many times that there are countless responses. Perhaps my favorite is to ask, if I'm descended from Germans, why are there still Germans? I think it hits on several key points in one example. First, it's obvious that I'm not descended from any living Germans. You have to go back several generations to find my most recent German ancestry. So, modern day Germans and I share a common ancestor. I'm not descended from modern day Germans. Quite literally, modern day Germans are my distant cousins, and modern day monkeys are my even more distant cousins. Related to that, the German culture of my ancestors back in Germany wasn't the same as modern day German culture. Once my family split away from our German relatives, my family's culture developed independently here in the U.S., while my cousins’ culture developed differently in Germany. Likewise, when we say that humans are descended from monkeys, those ancient species of monkeys weren't the same as modern day species of monkeys. We took one evolutionary path, and they took another. Further, this analogy shows that there's not necessarily a single ideal form that culture will develop towards, or by analogy, any single ideal form that animals will evolve towards. I'm sure American and German patriots will argue over which country is better (I actually do have very good German friends, and yes, we do argue about this good naturedly over beers), but both nations exist and are fairly successful. Looking back to the animal kingdom, there are lots of food sources, lifestyles, and niches for animals to survive in, including monkeys. Species will diversify to take advantage of all this variety of niches. There's no reason to suspect that other monkeys or apes would evolve to be more like people when they're already finding success in their own different ways. (There's also the competitive exclusion principle that predicts that no two species in the same environment will occupy the same niche.) Anyway, the next time somebody asks you that question, don't laugh at them or ridicule them. That's simply a surefire way to shut down any learning opportunity. Instead, take it as a teaching moment, and share a bit of the excitement of this topic.

Question: Why is there so much debate over the math question 12÷2(2+4) =?
Answer: A few other answers have said it's because the expression is ambiguous. But that's not really it. The expression isn't ambiguous at all. As an engineer myself, there's only one way to interpret that expression correctly. No. The issue is that lots of folks' exposure to math doesn't go much if at all beyond the high school level, and simplistic understandings of order of operations like PEMDAS or BODMAS. They don't know any further conventions that affect order of operations. The thing that makes this expression completely unambiguous is that there's no symbol in between the 2 and the parenthesis. That makes it clear that 2(2+4) is a single unit that can't be broken up. So the only appropriate way to interpret this expression is: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) What might have made this expression a bit ambiguous would have been to add a multiplication symbol: 12÷2×(2+4) Then it could be conceivable to interpret it a bit differently, perhaps instead as: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) However, even then, many engineers might interpret it the first way, keeping 2×(2+4) as a single unit as the denominator of the fraction. The reason is that when you're writing math 'inline' as opposed to formatting it the way math should really be written, division symbols are often treated as the fraction bar, with everything to the left assumed to be the numerator, and everything to the right assumed to be the denominator, and not cluttering things up with parentheses. As just one example, here are the definitions of some coefficients from one of my own engineering books, which I can assure you follow the convention that I just described (“my own” is in I own it, not that I wrote it). Really, if you wanted it to be 12/2, you'd probably put the parentheses around that to make it clear that 12/2 was a fraction, and instead write something like: (12/2)(2+4) But just to summarize, the expression as written in the original question isn't ambiguous. The issue is that lots of folks with only limited exposure to math don't know all the conventions affecting order of operations. And if there ever are any questions about ambiguity in an expression you’re writing, don’t be afraid to use parentheses.

Question: What is the biggest flying vertebrate of all time?
Answer: Given the incompleteness of the fossil record in general, the fragmentary remains of certain species in particular, and the vagaries of trying to reconstruct an entire animal based solely on fossil skeletal remains, the best answer can only be an estimate, not definitive. There are still a few standouts worth discussing, all of them pterosaurs, and all within one particular family, the Azhdarchidae. ABOVE: From left to right – a typical person for comparison, Quetzalcoatlus northropi, Arambourgiania philadelphiae, Hatzegopteryx thambema, and Cryodrakon boreas; note that these reconstructions are not based on the most complete of remains CREDIT: Gabriel Ugueto SOURCE: https://malibestsk.xyz/product_details/22449788.html Quetzalcoatlus northropi Q. northropi may be the most well known of these. When I was growing up, Quetzalcoatlus was the undisputed king of flying vertebrates before those other fossils had been discovered (or at least properly identified – Cryodrakon was originally misidentified as a Quetzalcoatlus species). Unfortunately, as Mark Witton put it in the article, Quetzalcoatlus: the media concept vs. the science, "It's also only known from bits and pieces of a gigantic left wing and cannot be regarded as a well known animal." Reconstructions of Q. northropi are instead based on comparisons to its smaller cousin, Q. lawsoni (referred to as Q. sp in older literature before it was finally named in 2021) – we have found much more complete remains of that species. As such, many estimates are based on scaling up Q. lawsoni to the size of the wing bones found for Q. northropi. ABOVE: Doug Lawson holding the massive humerus of Q. northropi SOURCE: The Quetz Monograph Lives and Other News on Azhdarchid Pterosaurs — Tetrapod Zoology Anyway, referring to that same Mark Witton article, "recent estimates of its wingspan being in the region of 10 m [32.8 ft] and predicted body masses of 200-260 kg [440-575 lbs]." Arambourgiania philadelphiae There are only very fragmentary remains of this animal. Here's a diagram from Mark Witton to show just how little. Only the parts in white are known from actual remains – one neck vertebrae and a few fragments from the wing. The parts in gray are conjecture. Note that A. philadelphiae is the creature on the right, while Q. lawsoni (the smaller Quetzalcoatlus species) is shown on the left for comparison: ABOVE: Q. lawsoni on left, A. philadelphia on right SOURCE: Why the giant azhdarchid Arambourgiania philadelphiae needs a fanclub If you look at the Wikipedia description of the animal, you find winspan estimates anywhere from 7-13 m (23-43 ft), though many pterosaur experts feel the higher side is an overestimate. In that same article from Mark Witton that I pulled the above figure from, he made a casual comment of a body mass in the range of 200-250 kg (440-550 lbs). Hatzegopteryx thambema Hatzegopteryx is know from a bit more fossil material. Here's a similar figure to the one above, which includes this species. It includes Q. lawsoni on the left, A. philadelphiae on the right, and H. thambema front and center. The figure uses the same conventions of white for known material, and gray for conjecture. 2BNaish%2Band%2BWitton%2B2016.jpg ABOVE: Q. lawsoni on the left, A. philadelphiae on the right, and H. thambema front and center SOURCE: New paper: when the short-necked, giant azhdarchid pterosaur Hatzegopteryx ruled Late Cretaceous Romania These bones show Hatzegopteryx to have been much more robust than the other known Azhdarchids, with a much wider skull than other known Azhdarchid skulls. Combined with the fact that no large theropods are known from the sediments where the Hatzegopteryx fossils were found, this has led to the idea that it might have been an apex predator in its environment. Wingspan estimates for this creature range from 10-12 m (33-39 ft). Relying on Wikipedia for another weight estimate, it might have been somewhere between 180-250 kg (400-550 lbs). Cryodrakon boreas From the little I've been able to find about this animal, the fossil remains come from a few different individuals, including (but not limited to) a neck vertebrae from a juvenile, and another neck vertebrae from an adult comparable in size to Quetzalcoatlus northropi. The Wikipedia description does state that it appears to have been slightly more robust thatn Q. northropi, so perhaps a bit heavier. ABOVE SOURCE: Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology (@RoyalTyrrell) on X So, which one of these species was actually the biggest? Who can say? The fossil remains just aren’t complete enough to say anything definitive about even the individual animals they’re from, let alone variation within each species. But it is interesting that all of them seem to be bumping up against the same limits on wingspan and bodyweight, of somewhere in the neighborhood of 10 m (33 ft) and 225 kg (500 lbs). That seems to suggest that that's approaching the limit of how big pterosaurs could get and still be able to fly. So perhaps, even if we do find more giant pterosaurs in the future, they'll still be in the same ballpark. Most of the links provided in the above answer are worth reading if you want more details. Question: What scientific fact, study, or research do you base your claim of God’s non-existence? Not one of you non-believers has provided a more suitable answer greater than lack of proof or evidence. Believer's faith is in the Bible. What's yours based in?
Answer: There's a big difference between the capital G God of the Bible, and a more generic lower case g god or higher power. The generic higher power is more difficult to 'disprove', and it's in this sense that many atheists admit there's still a small possibility of a god existing. But the capital G God of the Bible? Well, we've got the Bible itself to look at, along with archaeology. I've written about such things many times on Quora, and it would be easy to turn this into a Gish Gallop. In fact, I've already written such a 'Gish Gallop' type answer, which itself includes many links to other answers and articles: The introduction to that question is as good a summary as any: In short, the Bible seems exactly like the type of collection of stories that would develop organically over generations within a bronze age to iron age culture, and nothing at all like an inerrant work inspired by an actual God. There are all types of indications and clues within the Bible itself of how it developed over the generations, including the people’s changing concept of Yahweh. The early parts in Genesis seem like just-so stories that obviously don't match history on a literal level, and later parts like Exodus and the conquest of the Holy Land don't match archaeological evidence. And on top of all that, there are some stories that are just absurd at face value. To list just one example here, I'll go with the Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions*. The Kuntillet Ajrud archaeological site dates to some time around the 8th century, B.C. It was most likely "an Israelite state-sponsored enterprise" (source: The Inscriptions of Kuntillet ‛Ajrud Through the Lens of Historical Research). Among the findings there are inscriptions and drawings mentioning El, Yahweh, Ba'al, and Yahweh's wife, Asherah. For example, one of these inscriptions (on Pithos A) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata. While another (on Pithos B) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Teman and [his†] Asherata. ABOVE: A projection drawing of Pithos A, which includes the wording, "I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata." SOURCE: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Projection-drawing-of-Pithos-A-Meshel-et-al-2012-87-Fig-524-147-Fig-65-tags_fig1_318275592 So, right off the bat, we have a depiction of Yahweh that predates the composition of much of the the Bible‡, and shows the belief that he had a wife. (And note that these weren't the only two such inscriptions from the site.) This shows that the precursor to monotheistic Judaism was a polytheistic religion, where Yahweh wasn't the only god or goddess. It's also significant that there were separate mentions of a Yahweh of Samaria and a Yahweh of Teman. At the very least, these types of localized centers of worship contradict the Biblical narrative that the worship of Yahweh had been centralized to the Temple of Jerusalem by that point. But, according to that paper I already linked to, the author believes these different Yahwehs actually represent different regional deities with "distinct cultic vessels, rituals and ceremonies". The Yahweh of Samaria was only concerned with Samaria, while the Yahweh of Teman was concerned only with Teman. And further, a certain amount of the Deuteronomistic influence§ in the Bible was trying to bring these disparate religions and customs together into a unified religion for all of Israel and Judah. As one more quick note, another inscription from the site contains what may be a version of the story of Moses and the Exodus, but, according to that same paper, with "marked differences compared to the canonical biblical story, confirming the assumption of scholars that biblical traditions developed gradually over many years." So, from the archaeological findings at Kuntillet Ajrud, we have evidence showing one of the steps in the development of Yahweh, as a local deity with a goddess for a wife, before he developed into the monotheistic God of all creation that most people are familiar with, now. We also have details showing that the Biblical narrative isn't completely trustworthy, since worship of Yahweh hadn't yet been centralized to the Temple at Jerusalem like the story claims. And as I said, that's just from one archaeological site. That other answer that I already linked to provides many, many more examples. If you don't feel like scrolling back up to the top of this answer, here's that link again for easy reference: Even More Info: If you want a really, really detailed explanation, I wrote a short book that I self-published, that you can download for free from my personal website (since it is available as a free download, I trust this isn't spam according to Quora's policies): Footnotes: * Portions of this section were adapted from a prior answer: † I included the 'his' in brackets in those quotes because some researchers think there's a possessive suffix attaching Asherat to Yahweh, while others think the suffix is actually just part of the name, Asherata. ‡ The composition of the Bible is a whole topic in itself, that I did cover in the previously linked 'Gish Gallop' answer. § That 'Deuteronomistic influence' is part of the same topic of the composition of the Bible.

Question: If you throw an object up into the air in a moving car, why doesn't it go flying backwards?
Answer: This gets to the heart of Newton's Laws of Motion. Although many of us engineers and other technical folks take them for granted, now, they really did go against people's common sense intuition. Living in an environment like we do, where friction is ever-present, many people intuitively feel that a force must be continuously applied to an object for it to continue moving. Newton's insight can be summed up in his famous first law (copied here from Wikipedia’s paraphrase): A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, except insofar as it is acted upon by a force. The reason why objects in our everyday lives always slow down is because they're always subjected to external forces that slow them down, namely friction and air resistance. If it wasn't for those external forces, once you started an object in motion, it would continue moving forever, or at least until some other force acted upon it. So, when you're riding along in a car, the car, you, and any other objects in the car are all moving along at some speed. Let's just say 60 mph for the sake of argument. So, if you throw an object up inside the car, what force is going to slow it down? All the air in the car is traveling along with you at that same 60 mph, so there won't be any drag. Nothing else is touching the object to impart friction. So there isn't any force in the horizontal direction to slow the object down, and it'll continue right along at that 60 mph. Now, in the vertical direction, you did throw the object up to begin with, which gave it a starting force and corresponding vertical speed. And then the force of gravity will continuously pull it down, which will initially slow its upward speed, and eventually result in an ever increasing downward speed until you catch it again. Assuming this object is something hefty enough to ignore the small amount of air resistance (i.e. not a feather), after it leaves your hand, the only significant force would be gravity. So if we were to draw what's known as a free body diagram, it would look like this: So, with a force in only one direction, that's the only direction in which speed will change. Now, if we threw the object out the window instead of keeping it inside the car, that's a whole different story. Ignoring any wind, the air outside the car is essentially motionless. So as soon as the object hits that air, there will be air resistance. Now, the object will have at least two forces acting on it – the air resistance and the gravity. So now, the object will change speed in both the vertical and horizontal directions. Gravity will pull it downwards, while the air resistance will slow it down relative to the car. So from your perspective in the car, it will go flying backwards. But, just to point out one more thing, consider it from the point of view of somebody standing by the side of the road watching you. When you threw the object out the window, they wouldn't see it go flying backwards. They would see you, the car, and the object all initially at 60 mph. Then, the object would slow down while you and the car kept on going at 60 mph. You'd all be moving forward, it's just that you and the car would be going faster than the object. The figure below is about dropping a bomb, but it shows basically the same thing: ABOVE: Notice the difference between the ‘Vacuum Trajectory’ (with no drag) vs. the ‘Actual Trajectory’ (with drag) SOURCE: CHAPTER-23-D Basically, the reason an object tossed in a car doesn't go flying backwards is because it was already moving at the same speed as you and the car, and there's no force to change that.

Question: How is it possible that every little detail required for life and the human species to exist on Earth just happened to happen naturally?
Answer: There's probably somewhere on the order of 100 billion planets in the Milky Way galaxy, with all types of varying conditions. Just by chance, some of those planets will be conducive to life, while others won't. But guess where the intelligent life is going to be, wondering why their planets just so happen to be so well suited for their evolution. Just say that "every little detail required for life and the human species to exist" on a planet is a one in a million chance. With 100 billion planets, that still means 100,000 planets in our galaxy with those conditions. Even if it's a one in a billion chance, that's still 100 such planets. We don't yet know enough about planets outside our own solar system to say how rare it is for such conditions to exist. But even if it is extremely rare, it just stands to reason that the organisms pondering such things will be on the life supporting planets. And of course, we evolved to fit our planet, not the other way around. If other planets harbor life but with slightly different conditions, that life will almost certainly follow a different evolutionary path, producing creatures that don't resemble us humans. Also, this is an extremely self-centered question. You might as well ask how Earth is so conducive to tapeworms, or mushrooms, or oak trees. I rather like humans myself, but we're not the end-all, be-all of life on this planet. Heck, by biomass, the Earth really is a planet optimized for microbes, with us multicellular creatures just adding a bit of variety to the fringes.

Question: Is it possible to be both an atheist and a believer simultaneously? Have you ever met someone who identifies as both an atheist and a believer?
Answer: Going strictly by the definitions of the words, no. An atheist, by definition, is someone who lacks a belief in deities. So you can't logically be both an atheist and a believer in deities. However, people aren't always logical, nor do they always use words by their dictionary definitions. I've met one person in real life (and only one) who called themself an atheist, yet went on to describe how evil God was for allowing so much suffering in the world – and not in the way that someone like me treats God as a hypothetical or fictional character in a story, but actually stating it all as reality. While people like that are rare, they're not completely unheard of. Here are the results of a poll on atheists' beliefs in evolution: SOURCE: Religious Landscape Study Probably unsurprisingly, the vast majority of atheists accept evolution due to natural processes. But 2% of self-proclaimed atheists thought that evolution was due to God's design. So, while I don't want to pull a No True Scotsman, that guy and other folks like him aren't really atheists per the definition of the word, even if they do describe themselves as such. But, at least as far as self-identification, you can find people who call themselves atheists yet are nevertheless believers.

Question: Why are religious books deeper than novels?
Answer: Aside from the point many other answers have made, that religious books aren't necessarily as profound as some religious folks like to claim, the other aspect is Sturgeon's Law – Ninety percent of everything is crap. You often see this discussed in relation to more recent art and literature. The reason people have rose colored glasses about music from the ‘60s, ‘70s, ‘80s, etc. is that we only still listen to the 10% of the stuff that was good, and the 90% that was crap was relegated to the dustbins of history, while we haven't yet filtered out the 90% of the crap that constitutes modern day music. The same goes for ancient mythology and scriptures. The books now assembled in the Old Testament weren't the only stories floating around in Israel and Judah at the time. They were just the most popular ones that scribes decided to compile. Same thing with the Gospels and other books of the New Testament. For examples, here are lists from Wikipedia of books that didn't make it into the Bible: So, the Bible represents the best of the best of religious writings from that culture. It's not really fair to compare that to pulp fiction or novels about sparkly vampire stalking high school girls.

Question: Why can't English rugby be as popular as American football in the USA?
Answer: Well, they started off from the same roots, but then developed along independent paths in their respective countries. So it's no wonder that the version that developed in the USA is more popular in the USA. Both rugby and gridiron football, along with the various other types of football, grew out of a family of British games known as mob football, with different 'house rules' among every group in every town and village that played it. Since it was British colonists who were the first Europeans to come to what would become the U.S. and Canada, they brought along their British sports, including mob football. Round about the mid 1800s, social conditions were finally ripe to begin formalizing these diverse rules with different governing bodies. At the time, the Rugby School's rules were very similar to the rules at several American and Canadian colleges like Harvard, McGill, and Yale (in contrast to the association football rules of Cambridge and the Sheffield Football Club). The New World teams went on to develop new innovations that moved the sport further away from its cousin, rugby, including the line of scrimmage, a system of downs, and then in 1906 the forward pass (Walter Camp was especially influential in many of these innovations). ABOVE: An 1895 football game between Auburn and Georgia looking a lot more like rugby than modern day gridiron football SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia ABOVE: Another pre-forward pass college football game – the University of Minnesota vs. the University of Michigan in 1902 SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia So basically, the two sports started off largely the same, but then went down separate paths in each country. So of course the rules that developed in the USA are more popular here. If most Americans had wanted to play a game more similar to rugby, they wouldn't have changed the rules in the first place.

Question: How has technology changed our lives?
Answer: Technology essentially made our species possible. It's so ingrained into human existence that we barely even think about the most basic forms of technology, but we wouldn't be here without it. One of the most basic technologies, controlled use of fire, goes back at least around 1 million years. That predates Homo sapiens. It was probably Homo erectus that first developed that technology. Purposely shaped stone tools go back even further – 3.3 million years. That's before our ancestors had even evolved into the Homo genus. Those tools were probably made by something like Australopithecus afarensis or Kenyanthropus platyops. ABOVE SOURCE: Oldest stone tools pre-date earliest humans If you look at humans compared to a lot of other animals, while we're not as physically pathetic as some hyperbolic documentaries try to make us out to be, we're still on the slow, weak side when un-armed. But those ancient technologies that our ancestors developed allowed them to hunt, defend themselves, cook food, etc. That in turn allowed our ancestors to develop large, calorie hungry brains, while compensating with smaller muscles that didn't need as much nutrition as some of our bulkier cousins (I'm looking at you, gorillas, with your 5 to 10k calorie per day food requirements – The Influence of Seasonal Frugivory on Nutrient and Energy Intake in Wild Western Gorillas). Without that level of already existing technology in our pre-human ancestors, our own evolution just wouldn't have happened. And while we might consider those ancient technologies to be primitive, that's only from our spoiled perspective with our amazing modern technologies. You can see some uses of technology and tools in other animals, but our pre-human ancestors were already developing technologies beyond what other animals were doing. And by the time actual humans developed, there was a whole plethora of technologies – basket weaving, ropes, clothing, spears, etc. And once agriculture developed around 10k years ago and people could begin accumulating more possessions than just what they could carry, technology really took off. So how has technology changed our lives? By making our very existence possible.

Question: Does it bother atheists that people believe in God?
Answer: It does bother me that people believe in gods, but the extent to which it bothers me depends very much on the specifics of how the person acts. Look, most of my friends are Christians. And for the most part, we only discuss religion a bit, and have a live and let live attitude. As long as people are reasonable and tolerant, religion isn't the type of thing that gets me up in arms. But even then, it still bothers me some. I mean, I think back to when I was still a Christian, and all the cognitive dissonance I experienced, the fear of Hell (especially for others besides myself), the Catholic guilt, the wrestling with secular ethics vs. Biblical rules, etc. It may have taken me a few years to get to this point, but I'm happier now as an atheist than I was as a Christian, and I'd like for others to have that. But, I also don't want to be that guy that's always arguing and being pushy about beliefs. So here's a list of examples stepping through different types of believers and how I feel about them. Type of Believer: Tolerant believer who keeps their religion private and doesn't impose on others My Feelings: This bothers me on the same level as people who believe in urban legends, or who root for different sports teams from me. They're wrong about the nature of reality, and I would like to help them see the world more clearly, and recognize that the Steelers are the one true... sorry - wrong topic Level of Opposition: Good natured discussions over beer (though I hardly ever bring it up, waiting for others to broach the subject) Type of Believer: Somewhat tolerant believer, but who lets their religious beliefs influence the way they vote (particularly if they vote against women's rights or LGBT rights, or think global warming can't be real because God wouldn't let it happen) My Feelings: Well, now your religious beliefs aren't as private anymore, since they're having real world effects. So, now I do feel more justified in trying to get you to change your mind. Level of Opposition: More heated discussions over beer, Possible end of friendship depending on how they treat individuals Type of Believer: Door to door proselytizers My Feelings: Hoo boy. I love debate, and I have strong opinions on religion, and you actually came to my house with the purpose of talking about religion, so here we go. Level of Opposition: Debate for as long as they're willing to stay at my house Type of Believer: Parents who withhold real medical treatment from children in favor of faith healing My Feelings: I don't personally know anyone like this, but I know they're out there. The case of Makayla Sault was a heartbreaking, recent example. Children shouldn't have to suffer or die for the religious beliefs of their parents. Level of Opposition: Push for laws to outlaw this type of child abuse Type of Believer: Intolerant believer, who lets their religious beliefs influence the way they vote and how they treat individuals (particularly women, the LGBT community, and people outside their faith) My Feelings: Yeah, now they're definitely into the strong negative effects of religion, and I don't just feel justified to try to change their minds, but see it as a moral duty to society. Level of Opposition: Strong debate, definitely not going to be friends Type of Believer: Preachers/Leaders of Creationist/Evangelical/Fundamentalist Groups My Feelings: You're not just misleading yourself, but misleading all the people who follow you. And these brands of religion are usually the more close-minded branches that lead to negative effects, so I'm definitely going to speak up. Level of Opposition: Pointed blog entries and Quora answers Type of Believer: Intolerant Religious Politicians My Feelings: We have a First Amendment for a reason. Government and religion aren't supposed to be intertwined. It really, really bothers me when politicians pass religiously based laws, or give preferential treatment to certain religious institutions. Level of Opposition: Pointed blog entries and Quora answers, Vote for opponent So, that's how I feel about it. We live in a free, multicultural society, where people have the right to believe anything they want. As long as religious people are tolerant of others and don't use religion as a reason to discriminate or make bad decisions, the most they'll have to fear from me is talking about religion over a beer every once in a while. However, if a person's religious beliefs are having harmful, real-world consequences, then I'm going to speak up.
